title: Find the Minimum Amount of Time to Brew Potions
statement:
There are `n` wizards and `m` potions: wizard `i` has skill `skill[i]` and potion `j` holds `mana[j]` mana. Each potion is worked on by wizard `0`, then wizard `1`, and so on through wizard `n - 1`, and wizard `i` spends exactly `skill[i] * mana[j]` units of time on potion `j`.

- The potions are made in their given order: every wizard handles potion `0` first, then potion `1`, and so on, and never works on two potions at the same time.
- A potion may never wait between wizards: the moment one wizard finishes it, the next wizard must start on it.

Work begins at time `0`. Return the earliest time at which the last wizard can finish the last potion.
notes:
## Intuition

A potion never waits between wizards, so once its start at wizard 0 is fixed, its whole timetable is fixed. Starting every potion as early as possible is best, since an earlier potion never makes a later one wait longer. Trying start times and pushing them back after each clash works (that is the brute force), but one forward pass can find when the last wizard finishes the potion, and one backward pass then recovers when every other wizard finished it.

## Approach

1. `finish[i]` is when wizard `i` finishes its latest potion; all are `0` at first.
2. For the next potion, with mana `amount`, set `start` to `finish[0]`, when wizard `0` is free.
3. Walk forward: the potion reaches wizard `i` at `start + skill[i - 1] * amount`, but that wizard is busy until `finish[i]`, so keep the larger time. The delay shifts the whole timetable, so the potion still never waits.
4. The last wizard finishes at `start + skill[n - 1] * amount`.
5. Walk backward: wizard `i` hands the potion over exactly when wizard `i + 1` starts it, so `finish[i] = finish[i + 1] - skill[i + 1] * amount`.
6. After the last potion, return `finish[n - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

Potion 0 (`amount = 5`) meets no busy wizard: `finish = [5, 30, 40, 60]`. For potion 1 (`amount = 1`), `start` goes 5, then `max(6, 30) = 30`, `max(35, 40) = 40`, `max(42, 60) = 60`; the last wizard finishes at 64 and the backward pass gives `[53, 58, 60, 64]`. Potion 2 ends with `[58, 78, 86, 102]` and potion 3 with `[88, 98, 102, 110]`, so the answer is `110`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · m): two passes over the wizards per potion.
- Space: O(n) for `finish`.

## Pitfalls

- Delaying only the busy wizard would make the potion wait in between; the whole timetable must move.
- Keep the potions in their given order.
- One potion can take about 1.25 · 10^11 time units, so Java and C need 64-bit integers.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of wizards |
| `finish[i]` | when wizard `i` finishes its latest potion |
| `amount` | the current potion's mana |
| `start` | while walking forward, the earliest time wizard `i` can start the current potion |
| `i` | wizard index |

narration.3: finish[i] is when wizard i finishes its latest potion; nobody has worked yet.
narration.4: Brew the potions in their given order; amount is the current potion's mana.
narration.5: The potion can reach wizard 0 no earlier than when wizard 0 is free.
narration.6: Walk forward through the remaining wizards.
narration.7: The potion arrives when the previous wizard is done, but this wizard may still be busy; the later time wins, and the delay shifts the whole timetable.
narration.9: The last wizard finishes this potion after its own share of work.
narration.10: Now walk backward to find when every other wizard finished it.
narration.11: Wizard i hands the potion over exactly when wizard i + 1 starts on it.
narration.14: After the last potion, the last wizard's finishing time is the answer.
